items.title: The Shepherd's Word
items.moral: Moral: Our true wealth lies in an honest conscience and a word others can trust.
body: Once upon a time, in a village, there lived a poor but honest shepherd named Hasan. One day, the village chief called him and said:
“Hasan, I hear you know the mountain pastures well. Look after my herd this summer. If the animals come back healthy and well fed, I’ll give you a cow.”
Hasan agreed. All summer, through rain and sunshine, he tended the herd and kept watch at night. In the fall, he brought the animals home in excellent condition.
Hasan came to the chief, hoping to receive the promised cow. The chief smiled mockingly and said:
“I never meant to give you a cow. I only said that to make you work harder. Besides, what would a poor man like you do with one?”
Hasan's eyes filled with tears. But he answered calmly and with dignity:
“You’re right that I’m poor. But I have a conscience, and I keep my word. You may have money, but if your word has no value, you are poorer than I am.”
The story spread through the village. People lost respect for the chief and avoided doing business with him. Too late, he learned that a person’s worth rests on integrity, not wealth or position.

items.title: Spinach
items.moral: Moral: We often understand a mother's sacrifice in the face of impossibility years later. Love is sometimes hidden in a plate of simple food.
body: We lived in a remote village without even a proper road. My mother seemed obsessed with spinach. As a child, I sometimes wondered whether grief over my father’s death had unsettled her.

“You need to eat a lot, it gives strength to the body,” my mother would say, and for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, she would only feed us spinach, with a little cornbread on the side. I hated spinach already, I couldn’t stand to see this vegetable.
“When I’m grown and have a job and a family, there’ll be no spinach in my house,” I told her. She said she looked forward to that day and promised to dance at my wedding, however old she was.

The day came, I moved from our village to the city to study in high school. I somehow managed to make ends meet with the small scholarship I received. Once a month, when I came home, I didn't want to eat a spoonful of the spinach dish my mother put on the table. I only wanted to go back to the dormitory and eat delicious food.

I went on to university, then completed a master’s degree and a doctorate with government loans. By then, my mother was old and bent. When I returned to the village to marry, she kept her promise and danced at my wedding, tears streaming down her face. I did not understand those tears then.
Years passed. My mother passed away two years ago.

One day, I found an old notebook in a chest. In it, she had written: “All I had left were spinach seeds and a little corn to plant. There was no money. I cooked what I could grow so my children would not go hungry. I told them I served spinach three times a day because it was good for them. Saying it broke my heart. This was all I could do, though I loved them with everything I had.”

At fifty, I learned to love spinach. My wife wonders why I buy it so often. She thinks I like the taste. She does not know that its smell brings back my mother’s sacrifices and the sight of her dancing through tears at my wedding.

items.title: Lying
items.moral: Moral: Sometimes the kind words you tell yourself — “you can do it” — become the force that drives you forward. A person is as strong as he believes in himself.
body: “Do you ever lie?”
“Yes.”
“What about?”
“Only to myself. Every day I tell myself I’m stronger, more knowledgeable, and more capable than anyone else.”
“Perhaps you are.”
“No. There will always be people stronger or more capable than I am.”
“Then why say it?”
“Because it motivates me. It makes me want to learn, grow stronger, and keep improving.”

items.title: Three Scenes
items.moral: Moral: The three scenes warn against boasting of good deeds and growing accustomed to wrongdoing, while honoring the value of wise spiritual guidance.
body: On a journey, a young man witnessed three puzzling scenes.
First, he saw people sowing wheat that sprang up and ripened as soon as it touched the soil. Yet instead of harvesting it, the farmers burned the field.
Next, he saw a man struggling to lift a stone. Only after adding a second stone could he raise it. With a third, it became easier still. Bewildered, the traveler continued.
Finally, he saw a man riding a sheep, with others clinging to his shoulders. The sheep ran so swiftly that the people chasing it could not catch up.
At a city gate, he met a radiant old man and told him what he had seen. The elder explained:
“The farmers represent people who do good, then destroy its value by constantly boasting about it.
“The stones represent sin. The first wrongdoing weighs heavily. But without repentance, the next becomes easier, and the one after that easier still.

“The sheep is an animal of paradise, carrying its riders there. The first rider represents scholars, and those holding on are believers from every walk of life. Those left chasing behind are people without faith.”

items.title: We Are Rich
items.moral: Moral: True wealth is not in the treasury, but in the people’s well-being. A leader’s greatness lies not in the post, but in the meaning given to that post.
body: Near the end of the fourth century, Emperor Nintoku of Japan climbed a high tower one day and surveyed his country. Seeing not even a wisp of smoke rising, he realized his people were in poverty and that no one could cook at home.
He suspended taxes for three years and ordered that people work for their own households. He even sent the palace workers home. By the end of that time, the people were prospering.
Three years later Nintoku climbed the tower again, saw smoke rising on every side, and was sure that hearths were burning across the land. Joyfully he said to the lady beside him:
“Now we are rich!”
But the empress pointed to the palace, neglected for three years — roof leaking, flowers withered — and asked:
“You call this wealth?”
Nintoku’s answer has been remembered by the Japanese for centuries:
“When our people are poor, we are poor. When they prosper, so do we.”

items.title: Why Choose Injustice?
items.moral: Moral: When love, peace, friendship, and justice are possible, we are responsible for choosing them.
body: Haji Bektaş Veli:
Why hatred when there is love?
Why war when there is peace?
Why quarrel when there is brotherhood?
Why enmity when there is friendship?
Why intolerance when there is tolerance?
Why captivity when there is freedom?
Why injustice when there is justice?

items.title: The Woman and the Mirror
items.moral: Moral: We cannot control every change, but our outlook can help us meet it with good humor.
body: A woman wakes up in the morning and looks in the mirror. She sees that she has three strands of hair left on her head.
“I’ll braid my hair today,” she decided. She did, and had a lovely day.
The next day she wakes up and looks in the mirror again... She sees that she has two strands of hair left on her head.
“I’ll part it down the middle.” She did, and had another lovely day.
The next day she wakes up and sees that she has only one strand of hair left on her head.
“A ponytail today!” she said cheerfully, and enjoyed her day again.
Another day she looks in the mirror and sees that she has no hair left on her head.
“Wonderful!” she exclaimed. “Today I won’t have to do my hair at all.”

items.title: Work with Your Hands and Trust in Allah
items.moral: Moral: A person who looks at the share of the needy despite having the strength is not trusting in Allah - he is simply covering up his laziness with faith.
body: A dervish spent much of his time in prayer and solitude. He did not want to depend on others, so he also worked each day, buying bread with his earnings and sharing what remained with the poor.
One day in the desert, he saw a fox whose injured legs could barely carry it. “How does it survive?” he wondered. “It cannot hunt. How does Allah provide for it?”
Just then, a lion appeared with a gazelle in its jaws. It ate its fill and walked away. The fox crawled over and fed on what remained.

The dervish marveled at how Allah had provided for the fox. Then he thought, “If the fox receives food without working, why shouldn’t I? I could spend all my time in worship. Surely Allah will provide.”
He stopped working and prayed day and night. But no one brought food, and he grew weak and thin.
Finally, one day when he was exhausted, he heard a voice from the unseen:

“I gave you health and strength. Why choose the fox as your example instead of the lion? Rise and work. Earn your living, and let those who cannot help themselves find support in you. Feed yourself and others.”
Ashamed, the dervish repented and returned to work. Once more, he earned his bread and shared it, abandoning the wish to live at others’ expense.

items.title: Baklava
items.moral: Moral: Mocking another person’s poverty is among the gravest wrongs. Never forget that a mother may surrender her own share—even her final bite—for her child.
body: When I was a child, our family had very little money. One day, my father brought home some baklava, and we enjoyed it with tea that evening.
The next day was a holiday. My mother packed one piece of baklava, a few olives, and some bread for me to take to school.
My classmates had many different foods. A boy I disliked saw my modest meal and laughed:
“Did you bring that baklava for the mice?”
When the whole class laughed, I ran home in tears and shouted at my mother:
“Why did you give me only one piece? Everyone else had so much food—you humiliated me!”
My mother answered sadly:
“My child, that was my own piece.”

Her words broke my heart. She had saved her only piece of baklava for me instead of eating it herself. I was too ashamed even to hug her. Ever since, I have asked for forgiveness whenever I remember how I behaved. I have never been able to eat baklava again.
